Child assessment appointment planner

Bring a short history, examples from everyday life and your main questions. This printable planner organizes a conversation; it does not score or diagnose a child.

4 min read · Sources checked 26 October 2026 · Editorial information

Go to the worksheet

A developmental appointment can cover years of history in a short conversation. It is easy to remember a key question only after leaving, or to spend most of the visit trying to explain a broad concern such as “school is difficult”. This planner helps turn that concern into a few useful examples.

Use the guidance below to prepare, then print the blank worksheet. You do not need to complete every item or know which diagnosis to ask about. The most valuable preparation is an honest description of the child’s strengths, difficulties and everyday context.

What you will take away

  • Bring examples rather than a proposed diagnosis.
  • Include strengths, languages and the child’s own perspective.
  • Leave with a named next step and a review plan.

In this guide

  1. Before the visit: choose your main question
  2. Bring a balanced picture of the child
  3. During the appointment: clarify the recommendation
  4. After the visit: turn advice into a next step
  5. Printable worksheet
  6. Common questions

01

Before the visit: choose your main question

Write the concern in one sentence, then add one recent example. “My child struggles with transitions” becomes more useful when followed by “Leaving the playground takes about 20 minutes and often ends in tears, even after a verbal warning”. Describe the setting and what adults tried, without assigning blame.

Choose up to three questions you most want answered. Separate an urgent medical change from a longer-standing developmental concern. If there has been loss of skills, a seizure, sudden weakness or a child who is acutely unwell, seek appropriate medical advice promptly rather than waiting to finish this planner.

  • Read what to expect during developmental assessment

02

Bring a balanced picture of the child

Include enjoyable activities, successful situations and preferred ways of communicating. Mention the languages used by family members and school. A child may show different abilities with different people, so bring both accounts rather than deciding that one must be wrong.

List previous assessments, hearing or vision information if available, and current medicines and supplements. Product labels can prevent confusion over ingredients. Do not pay for a new test package just to arrive “fully prepared”; ask the clinician which investigations, if any, are needed. A concise summary is usually more useful than a large folder with no explanation of what matters.

Illustrative completed note

Main question: “How can school instructions be easier to follow?” Example: “P. manages one step at home but loses track of three-step spoken instructions in class.” Strength: “Enjoys drawing and follows picture sequences for craft.” Family goal: “Start the first classroom task with less distress.”

03

During the appointment: clarify the recommendation

Ask what each suggested assessment or therapy is intended to answer or improve. If a term is unfamiliar, request an everyday example. Ask whether recommendations are urgent, optional or dependent on another result. If the plan is more than the family can currently manage, say so; priorities should be discussed openly.

Where possible, include the child’s views and communication preferences. Ask how information will be shared with school and what consent is needed. A report can contain sensitive family or medical information that is not necessary for every teacher. It may be more appropriate to share the relevant support recommendations rather than the entire document.

04

After the visit: turn advice into a next step

Record who will arrange each referral, how results will be communicated and when to review. For a home or school strategy, agree a concrete goal and how you will notice improvement or increased distress. For medicine, follow the prescriber’s instructions and clarify how to report concerns.

Keep the completed sheet somewhere private. Bring it back to the next visit and mark what happened: completed, waiting, no longer needed or unclear. The sheet is a conversation aid, not a diagnostic test, and it should reduce the family’s administrative burden rather than create another task they must perform perfectly.

My appointment notes

Print this page or save it as a PDF using your browser. Write on the printed copy. This page does not collect your answers.

Child’s age, date and languages used

Strengths, interests and preferred ways to communicate

Main concern: one recent example and when it began

Any lost skills, illness or sudden change

Home and school observations; what helps

Sleep, eating, hearing, pain or movement concerns

Medicines and supplements, including product labels

Previous assessments or reports to bring

My three questions

Agreed next step, responsible person and review date

Common questions

Do I need a diagnosis to use this planner?

No. It is useful whenever you want to discuss a developmental concern.

Editorial information

This guide was developed from supplied teaching notes and the linked sources. Worked examples are fictional illustrations, not patient stories. No named clinician review has been recorded; this is general education rather than an individual assessment or prescription. The original presenters are not represented as authors or endorsers.
